articles.title: Horoscope for Tuesday, September 29, 2026
articles.description: Moon alert Avoid shopping (except food and gas) and important decisions after 6 p.m. Chicago time. The moon is in Taurus. Aries (March 21-April 19) An average day Today you might find that you identify with your possessions more than usual. In fact, this could be why you might be tempted to be a bit extravagant or go overboard buying something. This same sense of largess might creep into your financial negotiations. Be aware of this. Taurus (April 20-May 20) A positive day This is a positive day for you because the moon is in your sign, dancing beautifully with lucky Jupiter. Keep in mind that you love antiques and beautiful things, and today, your financial judgment might be a bit off because of a tendency to be extravagant. "I'll take both!" Gemini (May 21-June 20) A positive day This is a playful time for you, which is why you will enjoy social outings, vacations, sports events, the arts and fun activities with kids. Basically, you want to enjoy yourself. Your positive communication style might attract others today because enthusiasm is contagious. Cancer (June 21-July 22) An average day Be careful about going overboard with financial matters today. You might spend too much. You might give too much away. This is because there's an aspect of "excess" influencing your financial decisions. Remember, true generosity is giving what is needed. Leo (July 23-Aug. 22) An average day Be aware that you're high-viz today, which means people notice you more than usual. In fact, some people know personal details about your private life. Others see you as confident but also benevolent and compassionate. This is good. Virgo (Aug. 23-Sept. 22) An average day Today, you might be more attracted than usual to philosophical ideas, religion and lofty topics that make you think about life and how things are and how they should be. You might examine other people's attitudes toward politics and religion. (You're the most observant sign in the zodiac.) Libra (Sept. 23-Oct. 22) An average day You are a people-oriented sign, and today, you feel generous to friends and members of groups. In fact, if making a decision about how to share something or divide an inheritance, make sure to protect your own self-interest and not give away the farm. Scorpio (Oct. 23-Nov. 21) An average day This is an excellent day for you to shop for wardrobe goodies, although please be aware of the restrictions of the moon alert. Whether shopping or in discussions with partners and close friends, guard against going overboard. Don't make promises you can't keep. If shopping, keep your receipts. Sagittarius (Nov. 22-Dec. 21) An average day Work-related travel might happen for many of you today. Whatever you do, whether it's with your work, your health or dealing with a pet, you'll be inclined to think big and be extravagant. However, you will also want to be benevolent, which is a good thing. Always seek the highest good. Capricorn (Dec. 22-Jan. 19) A positive day This is a wonderful, fun-loving day for you! Enjoy socializing, partying and the arts, especially theater, movies and galleries. Sports events and playful times with children will please you. Romance is blessed. This is also a good day for financial speculation if you're aware of the moon alert. Aquarius (Jan. 20-Feb. 18) A positive day "Hail fellow, well met!" Your interactions with others will be friendly and mutually rewarding because people are openhearted and generous today. These pleasant interactions will take place with partners, close friends and people at home, as well as members of the general public. Pisces (Feb. 19-March 20) A positive day You feel confident, enthusiastic and ready to grab the world by the tail — but don't bite off more than you can chew today, especially in discussions with others and making promises or commitments. If today is your birthday Actor Ben Miles (1966) shares your birthday. You're imaginative, sensitive and idealistic. You're also perceptive, practical and ready to help. This year is about socializing and having fun because your creativity, zest and desire for life are at a pinnacle. Let your guard down, and loosen up a bit. Old friends might reappear to rekindle relationships.

articles.title: Saving the Siamese crocodile: Cambodia moves to protect one of the world’s last wild populations
articles.description: Indigenous communities play crucial role, as ‘genetic bank’ area of wetland offers hope for critically endangered reptile In the 1990s, conservationists in Cambodia feared the Siamese crocodile had disappeared for good. Fishing and hunting had devastated the species throughout the 20th century, leaving populations across its native south-east Asia on the brink of extinction. But in villages dotted among the wetlands of the remote Cardamom mountains, Indigenous Chorng communities still reported seeing them. Passing this knowledge to researchers surveying the area in 2000 led to an official recording of the species – and bolstered the mission to revive the population. Continue reading...

articles.title: Himalayan diplomacy: A new frontier for Pakistan–Nepal climate cooperation
articles.description: Somewhere above 4,500 metres in Gilgit-Baltistan, a glacier that has fed the Indus for millennia is losing ice faster than at any point since scientists began keeping records. A thousand kilometres to the east, in the Khumbu region of Nepal, the same story is unfolding on the slopes below Everest. Two countries, separated by India’s landmass and decades of diplomatic distance, are quite literally standing on the same melting ground. It is time Islamabad and Kathmandu recognised what geography has been telling them all along: their futures are tied together by ice, water and risk, and neither can afford to keep looking at the mountains alone. The numbers are no longer abstract. Research from the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD), the Kathmandu-based body that has monitored the Hindu Kush Himalaya for half a century, found that glaciers across the region have lost as much as 27 metres of ice thickness since 1975, with the rate of loss having doubled since the turn of the century. Pakistan alone is home to roughly 13,000 glaciers, and the Indus, the river that irrigates the bulk of Pakistani agriculture and sustains its hydropower, draws an extraordinary 70 per cent of its flow from glacier and snowmelt. Nepal’s glaciers, including the closely watched Mera and Rikha Samba, serve the same role for South Asia’s eastern river systems. When ICIMOD’s scientists call this region the “Third Pole” and the “Water Tower of Asia”, they are not being poetic. They are describing the plumbing that keeps nearly 2 billion people alive. Pakistan has already paid the price of treating this as someone else’s problem. The 2022 floods were not simply an unlucky monsoon. The country received close to 190pc of its normal July-August rainfall, with Sindh and Balochistan hit by rainfall multiples far beyond historical norms, and the result was catastrophe: over 1,700 dead, 33 million people affected, roughly a third of the country under water, and a UN-backed Post-Disaster Needs Assessment putting total damages and economic losses above $30bn, with reconstruction needs exceeding $16bn. Pakistan’s government and independent assessments alike have pointed to a common driver behind that disaster, a warming Himalayan and Karakoram system dumping glacial meltwater into rivers already swollen by erratic rain. This is precisely the “compound risk” that ICIMOD hydrologists have flagged in the region more broadly: rising temperatures, unstable slopes and unpredictable rainfall no longer arrive as isolated events but stack on top of one another, as seen even in this year’s flash flooding in Gilgit-Baltistan’s Thore Valley. Nepal understands this compounding danger as well as any country on earth. It has spent years building glacial lake outburst flood monitoring systems, evacuation protocols for high-altitude valleys, and community-based early warning networks precisely because its mountain villages have nowhere to run when a lake bursts. Pakistan, meanwhile, has real operational experience of its own, in flood forecasting for the Indus basin, in cold-climate agricultural adaptation, and in managing glacier-fed irrigation systems that are among the most extensive in the world. Put simply: Nepal has hard-won expertise in glacial hazard monitoring, and Pakistan has hard-won expertise in managing the downstream consequences at a massive scale. Neither country has had to build both halves of this puzzle alone before, and neither should have to now. This is where a bilateral climate framework, modest in ambition but serious in substance, makes sense. Islamabad and Kathmandu could begin with something achievable: a joint glacier and hydrology monitoring exchange, building on the scientific groundwork ICIMOD has already laid across its eight member states. Pakistani meteorological and irrigation authorities could share Indus basin flood-forecasting models with Nepal’s disaster management agencies, while Nepal’s glacial lake outburst flood expertise could inform Pakistan’s own early-warning systems for the roughly 3,000 glacial lakes identified in its northern territories, some of which are classified as dangerously unstable. None of this requires reinventing diplomatic wheels. It requires Pakistan to assert, clearly and confidently, that it is a mountain nation with mountain interests, not merely a downstream victim waiting for the next disaster, but a serious technical partner capable of shaping how South Asia adapts. There is also a quieter strategic logic here. Pakistan has long been boxed into a regional conversation dominated by its relationship with India, one that leaves little room for the kind of functional, low-politics cooperation that climate diplomacy allows. Nepal, similarly, has often been treated as a subject of Indian and Chinese strategic competition rather than an actor. A Pakistan–Nepal climate channel sidesteps that framing entirely. It is not about alliances or rivalries; it is about rivers, ice, and the shared arithmetic of survival. That makes it precisely the kind of cooperation both nations can pursue without inviting the usual regional anxieties and precisely the kind of cooperation that lets Pakistan demonstrate leadership on an issue where it has genuine standing to speak. The Hindu Kush Himalaya assessment that ICIMOD produced years ago carried a blunt warning: even if the world holds warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius, the region will still lose roughly a third of its glacier volume by century’s end; under weaker climate action, that loss could reach two-thirds. Pakistan does not have the luxury of waiting to see which scenario unfolds. Every flood season narrows the window for building the kind of resilient, cooperative infrastructure that could soften the next disaster instead of merely responding to it. Himalayan diplomacy will not solve Pakistan’s water and climate vulnerabilities on its own. But it offers something rarer than a solution: a genuine, forward-looking partnership built on shared mountains rather than shared grievances. Pakistan should seize it, not as a favour to Nepal, but as an act of enlightened self-interest for a nation that lives, quite literally, downstream of the Third Pole. Header image: View of the landscape from Langtang, Nepal can be seen in this undated handout file photo. — Tika Gurung via Reuters

articles.title: The endangered wild ponies of Eriskay in the Outer Hebrides – a photo essay
articles.description: Fewer than 400 Eriskay ponies remain. One of the rarest native breeds in the world, their plight is unique because the community living on their tiny Hebridean island are fighting for them. The ponies wander the village and townsfolk care for them together On the slopes of Beinn Sciathan, a rocky outcrop in the Outer Hebrides, white and grey ponies roam freely. Eriskay ponies, one of the rarest native breeds in the world, are critically endangered. They have often been mixed with the Highland pony and other breeds, giving the false impression of higher population numbers. Only about 300 to 400 true Eriskay ponies are thought to remain.
